newsitem.title: GERMANY: German employers determined to lower labour costs.
newsitem.headline: German employers determined to lower labour costs.

text.p: German employer groups on Wednesday reaffirmed their determination to lower labour costs despite the rising threat of industrial unrest in key industries such as the metal and engineering sector.

There were also signs that Germany's long-standing system of collective wage bargaining was increasingly being seen as too inflexible to bring about the labour cost-savings employers say are urgently needed.

IG Metall, the country's most powerful trade union, had said on Tuesday it would not rule out strikes early next year following the collapse of negotiations aimed at finding agreement on proposed sick pay cuts.

But Dieter Hundt, incoming president of the German Federation of Employers Associations, said cuts to sick payments were only the first of a number of steps employers would need to make to regain competitiveness.
"There must still be significantly more made," Hundt told an employers' conference in Berlin entitled "Strengthening Competitiveness, Securing Jobs".

Hundt said German companies had seen their unit wage costs increase 20 percent faster than their main rivals abroad over the last seven years. In particular he blamed cuts to the working week without a lowering of wages.
Such arguments were vigorously rejected by unions, who said their case was strengthened by a Bundesbank report that recent moderate wage agreements would help corporate profits for 1996.

The debate over labour costs in Germany has taken on a new feverishness in recent weeks after a law was passed cutting sick pay from full salary to 80 percent -- a move designed to save German firms around 12 billion marks ($7.87 billion) a year.

Early attempts by companies such as Daimler-Benz to implement the law were thwarted by huge protests by metal and engineering workers, who see sick pay and other benefits as prizes for concessions in past wage rounds.
But Bernhard Jagoda, president of Germany's Federal Employment Office said Germany's relatively high wages were increasingly not being justified by higher productivity.
"Our goal must be to fit wage policy more closely to productivity again," Jagoda told the employers' conference.

Jagoda said it was time for more flexibility to be introduced into the collective wage bargaining system that is widely held to have served Germany well in its post-war recovery. Future industry-wide wage agreements should leave
more room for adaptation by individual companies according to their needs, he added.

Jagoda's comments came as Werner Stumpfe, president of the Gesamtmetall metal and engineering employers federation, warned that a collectively-negotiated settlement of the sick pay dispute could now no longer be possible.
Stumpfe told a news briefing that if further attempts to seek agreement on the new law failed, "We will have to do without a standard clause (on sick pay) altogether."

Individual German companies would then have to negotiate their own agreements with their workers in a development that some economists believe could be the beginning of the end of collective wage agreements.
